title: Metals vs non-metals
keyIdea: Metals are usually shiny when clean, conduct heat and electricity well, are malleable (they bend and flatten instead of breaking) and ductile (they can be drawn into wire), and often ring when struck (sonorous). Solid non-metals are usually dull and brittle, and most are insulators. Metal oxides are basic, so the soluble ones make alkalis in water; non-metal oxides are acidic. No single test decides: iodine is shiny but brittle, graphite conducts but carbon is a non-metal, mercury is a liquid metal, and only iron, nickel and cobalt are magnetic. On the periodic table, metals sit to the left of the staircase line and in the middle block, non-metals to the right, with hydrogen the odd one out.
familyTip: Hunt for metals in the kitchen. Tap a spoon and a pan lid to hear them ring, check which ones a fridge magnet sticks to (steel yes, aluminium foil and copper-bottomed pans no), and look at the pencil lead (graphite) in a pencil: a non-metal that conducts.

visual.caption: A property of most metals, or of most non-metals? Drag each card, or tap it and then tap a box.

lab.caption: Flagship lab: test elements in a circuit, with a hammer and with a magnet, weigh tricky evidence, find the staircase, test oxides in indicator.

kid: Most elements are metals. Copper, iron and aluminium are shiny when clean. They let heat and electricity pass through them easily. Hit them and they bend or flatten instead of breaking. We call that malleable. Many ring like a bell when struck.
Non-metals are different. Solid ones such as sulfur are dull and brittle, so a hammer shatters them. Most do not conduct electricity. Many non-metals, such as oxygen and nitrogen, are gases.

One test is not enough. Iodine is shiny, but it shatters and does not conduct. Graphite, a form of carbon, conducts, but carbon is a non-metal. Mercury is a metal that is liquid. Only iron, nickel and cobalt stick to a magnet.

The periodic table shows the pattern. Metals are on the left and in the middle. Non-metals are on the right of a staircase line. Hydrogen is the odd one out at the top left. Burn a metal and its oxide makes an alkali in water. A non-metal oxide makes an acid.
adult: Ages 11 to 13. The KS3 science curriculum (DfE 2013) asks for the properties of metals and non-metals, and for how their oxides behave as acids or bases. About three in four elements are metals. Key words: malleable (bends and flattens), ductile (can be drawn into wire), sonorous (rings), conductor, insulator, brittle.

These properties are trends, not rules, so your child should look at several of them together. The well-known odd ones out: mercury is a liquid metal, sodium is soft, graphite is a non-metal that conducts, iodine is a shiny non-metal, and diamond is a very hard non-metal. The oxide test is firmer. Metal oxides such as magnesium oxide are basic. Non-metal oxides such as sulfur dioxide are acidic.

Common mistakes: thinking all metals are magnetic (only iron, nickel, cobalt and steel are); deciding from shine alone; thinking only metals conduct; thinking every metal is a hard solid; calling hydrogen a metal because it sits above group 1; and thinking metal oxides make acids. The lab tests each one.

In the lab your child puts 5 elements in a circuit, hits 5 with a hammer and tests 5 with a magnet. Then they sort 6 tricky elements by weighing the evidence, place 6 elements either side of the staircase line, and drop 4 oxides into universal indicator to read the pH.

practice.prompt: Element X is shiny, bends without breaking and conducts electricity. What is it most likely to be?
practice.hint: Count how many properties point the same way.
practice.explain: Shiny, malleable and a conductor: all three point to a metal.

practice.prompt: Which of these is a non-metal that conducts electricity?
practice.hint: Think of the grey 'lead' inside a pencil.
practice.explain: Graphite is a form of carbon, a non-metal, but it conducts. Sulfur is an insulator, and copper is a metal.

practice.prompt: A class tests {a} metal objects with a magnet. Only {b} of them are made of iron or steel. How many objects do not stick?
practice.hint: Only iron, nickel, cobalt and steel stick. Take those away from the total.
practice.explain: {a} objects minus the {b} iron or steel ones leaves {=a-b} that do not stick, even though they are all metals.

practice.prompt: An oxide dissolves in water with universal indicator and gives pH {a}. How many pH units is that above neutral (pH 7)?
practice.explain: pH {a} is {=a-7} above 7, so the solution is alkaline. That is what a metal oxide does.

practice.prompt: Sulfur dioxide dissolves in water with universal indicator. What colour do you expect?
practice.hint: Sulfur is a non-metal. What do non-metal oxides make in water?
practice.explain: Non-metal oxides are acidic. Sulfur dioxide makes an acid of about pH 3, so the indicator turns red or orange.

pool.prompt: Iodine has shiny grey crystals. Why is it classed as a non-metal?
choices: It is brittle and does not conduct
pool.hint: Shine is one property. What do the other tests show?
pool.explain: Iodine shatters when hit and is an insulator. Shine alone does not make something a metal.

pool.prompt: Will a magnet pick up a strip of pure aluminium?
pool.hint: Which metals are magnetic? There are only three common ones.
pool.explain: Only iron, nickel and cobalt (and steel) are magnetic. Aluminium is a metal that a magnet does not pull.

pool.prompt: Where are the metals on the periodic table?
choices: Left of the staircase line and in the middle block
pool.explain: Metals fill the left side and the middle block. Non-metals are right of the staircase, plus hydrogen.

pool.prompt: Why are saucepans often made of aluminium or steel?
choices: They conduct heat well and do not shatter
pool.hint: A pan has to pass heat to the food and survive being knocked.
pool.explain: Metals conduct heat well and are malleable, so a pan heats the food and bends rather than breaking.

pool.prompt: A class puts {a} samples in a circuit. {b} of them light the bulb. How many samples are insulators?
pool.hint: The ones that light the bulb conduct. Take them away from the total.
pool.explain: {a} samples minus {b} conductors leaves {=a-b} insulators. Most of those will be non-metals.

pool.prompt: Mercury is a liquid at room temperature. Is it a metal?
choices: Yes: it is shiny and conducts
No: it is a liquid, so it is neither
pool.hint: Being liquid is one property. Check the others.
pool.explain: Mercury is shiny and a good conductor, so it is a metal, the only one that is liquid at room temperature.

pool.prompt: A copper wire carries a current of {a} A. A strip of sulfur in the same circuit carries 0 A. What is the difference in current in amps?
pool.hint: Sulfur is an insulator, so its current is 0. Subtract.
pool.explain: {a} minus 0 is {a} A. Copper conducts and sulfur does not.

pool.prompt: Magnesium burns to make magnesium oxide. What does the oxide do in water with universal indicator?
pool.hint: Magnesium is a metal. What kind of oxide do metals make?
pool.explain: Metal oxides are basic. Magnesium oxide gives about pH 10, so universal indicator turns blue.

pool.prompt: Hydrogen sits above group 1 on many periodic tables. What is it?
pool.hint: Does hydrogen look shiny, or conduct, at room temperature?
pool.explain: Hydrogen is a colourless gas that does not conduct: a non-metal, the exception on the left of the table.
